title: Sex differences in human fatigability: mechanisms and insight to physiological responses
population: Review of neuromuscular fatigability literature in men and women
findings: Women are usually less fatigable than men for similar-intensity isometric fatiguing contractions, but the difference is task specific.
Task variables that alter the sex difference include type, intensity and speed of contraction, muscle group and environmental conditions.
Proposed mechanisms include motor neurone pool activation, metabolically sensitive small afferent input, muscle perfusion and metabolism, and fibre type properties.
A sex bias toward studying males masks true understanding of magnitude and mechanisms; the review states there is a tremendous lack of understanding of sex differences in fatigability.
limitations: Narrative review, mostly isometric laboratory tasks rather than running; no running effect sizes in the abstract.
implications: Fatigue resistance is task dependent, so no universal female fatigue-resistance factor belongs in run load models.
Keep sex out of the fatigue/recovery model as a multiplier; use the individual's session RPE, HR drift and wearable recovery data.

verification.notes: Crossref matches (Acta Physiol, 2014-02, Hunter). Europe PMC abstract (PMID 24433272) supports all findings; no numbers.
